clue.text: Batsman with shot that manifests his calling

parts.note: Ian Bell was an England Test batsman
a pull is a cricket stroke hitting the ball to leg

explanation.surface: A cricketer's favourite stroke reveals his true vocation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calling' looks like vocation, but here it is summoning a servant: the handle someone tugs shows they are calling. In cricket, a pull is a shot played across the line to the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellpull is the cord or handle a householder tugs to summon staff, so it makes their calling evident.

clue.text: See 24 across
Foreign metal in a roll raised iconic building

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the assembled letters are read from the bottom up
the metal goes inside the roll

parts.note: a bap is a soft bread roll
fer is French for iron

explanation.surface: Some exotic metal baked into a bread roll was held up by an iconic structure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign' signals a French word, and 'raised' reads upward in a down clue. A bap is a British soft bread roll; prefabs were mass-built after the war.
explanation.definitionFit: Factory-made prefabricated houses became an iconic image of postwar British housing.

clue.text: Queen Street characters coming one after another

indicators.note: the letters of the words are taken as characters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A London address whose residents arrive in turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' turns QUEEN plus ST (street) into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Sequent is a formal adjective for following in order, successive.

clue.text: In which it appears that Queen's may be turned

definitions.text: In which it appears that Queen's may be turned

parts.words: In which it appears that Queen's may be turned
parts.note: an accomplice who testifies against confederates is said to turn Queen's something; it is also what appears in court as proof

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark about a monarch being swung round.
explanation.walkthrough: In British law a criminal who testifies against accomplices in exchange for leniency 'turns Queen's evidence'.
explanation.definitionFit: Proof presented in court is what appears there, and the idiom pairs it with turning Queen's.

clue.text: Order to breeder coming round after time assumed

parts.note: PO is a postal order

indicators.note: the stud surrounds the other piece, coming round it

parts.note: a stud is a stallion or farm kept for breeding
late means after the expected time

explanation.surface: An instruction sent to an animal breeder arrived round after hours, it was supposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a command but is a postal order; 'to' just links, and 'after time' means overdue.
explanation.definitionFit: To postulate is to take something as given, so postulated means taken for granted or supposed.

clue.text: Small boy embracing model to be acquitted

indicators.note: the boy's name holds the model inside it

parts.note: Geoff is a shortened form of the boy's name Geoffrey
the Model T was the Ford car

explanation.surface: A little lad hugs a fashion model in order to be let off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' suggests a catwalk; it is the Ford Model T, giving T.
explanation.definitionFit: To get off is to escape conviction or punishment in court.

clue.text: Revolutionary turns into little helper for suckers

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go inside the small word

parts.note: wee is Scots for little

indicators.note: a revolutionary overturns things, so the following word is rearranged

explanation.surface: An insurgent changes into a small assistant for gullible people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a person but rearranges the next word. 'Suckers' sounds like dupes; it means suckling babies.
explanation.definitionFit: A wet nurse breastfeeds another woman's baby, helping infants who suckle.

clue.text: See 19
See 24 down
Cosmetic base for trust in the NHS

definitions.meaning: make-up applied first, as a base layer
some NHS hospitals are run as self-governing bodies of this named kind of trust

explanation.surface: Make-up groundwork for a health service body.
explanation.walkthrough: The NHS is Britain's National Health Service; many of its hospitals are run by 'foundation trusts'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a base layer of make-up and an endowed institution or trust.

clue.text: Uproar in the nave by American boy

parts.note: the nave of a wheel is its hub
bub is American slang for a boy or man

explanation.surface: A commotion in the church nave caused by a youngster from the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nave' suggests a church; here it is the old word for the centre of a wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A hubbub is a loud confused noise, a commotion.

clue.text: Flier gets increasingly religious eating very posh biscuit

parts.note: a bat is a flying mammal

indicators.note: the comparative swallows the abbreviation inside it

parts.note: holier means more pious

explanation.surface: A flying creature grows more devout while munching a smart biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: A Bath Oliver is a plain dry English biscuit, named after a Bath doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Bath Olivers are an upmarket English savoury biscuit, often eaten with cheese.

clue.text: 16 shows result of search in cupboard for bone

definitions.text: 16 shows result of search in cupboard for bone

parts.words: 16 shows result of search in cupboard for bone
parts.note: the nursery rhyme cupboard was bare; and if politics is all on the right, the opposite side is empty

explanation.surface: Mother Hubbard's fruitless hunt for a dog's bone.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 is ALL RIGHT: if everyone is right, nobody is left. Old Mother Hubbard went to her cupboard to fetch her dog a bone and found it bare.
explanation.definitionFit: When the cupboard is bare there is nothing remaining, and when all are right, nobody is on the left.

clue.text: Spooner's pet's entry to working-class symbol

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words

parts.note: a cat is a household pet
a flap is a small door letting an animal in

explanation.surface: The way a household animal gets in becomes an emblem of the working man.
explanation.walkthrough: A cat's flap with its openings swapped. The flat cap is the cloth cap stereotypically worn by British working men.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth cap is the classic emblem of the British working man, as in 'cloth cap and whippet'.

clue.text: 7 holding both sides? No problem

indicators.note: the synonym for the 7 answer contains the pair of letters

parts.note: the 7 answer means to get down from a vehicle, as alight does
left and right, L and R

explanation.surface: Someone escaping a charge clings on to both camps, and says that's fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 7 is GET OFF, which here means alight from a bus. 'both sides' are left and right.
explanation.definitionFit: All right is an assenting reply meaning that's fine, no trouble at all.

clue.text: Hence came Dame Dench, a class act: forlorn hope tangling with that

indicators.note: the words are knotted together into a new order

explanation.surface: A famous actress came from here: a fine performer mixing with a lost cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tangling' rearranges all 29 letters of DAME DENCH, A CLASS ACT and FORLORN HOPE; 'with that' just links. Judi Dench trained at this London drama school.
explanation.definitionFit: Judi Dench trained at the Central School of Speech and Drama in London, so it is the place she came from.

clue.text: Freedom encourages my aunt to keep ducks

indicators.note: read as en-courages, putting the letters through their paces in a new order

parts.note: a duck is a cricket score of nothing, so two ducks are two Os, kept among the aunt's letters

explanation.surface: Independence spurs on my aunt to keep some waterfowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'encourages' rearranges MY AUNT together with OO, the two ducks it is told 'to keep'. A duck is a cricket score of nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Autonomy is self-government, independence, the freedom to act on one's own.

clue.text: Demon gripping Clive on a bender with indoor plant

indicators.note: the demon holds the rearranged letters inside

parts.note: an afrit is an evil spirit in Arabian myth

indicators.note: a bender is a drinking spree, so the letters lurch into a new order

explanation.surface: A fiend grabs a drunken Clive, who has a houseplant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on a bender' looks like one phrase, but 'on a' belongs with Clive as fodder and 'bender' alone is the signal; 'gripping' puts the result inside the demon.
explanation.definitionFit: The African violet, Saintpaulia, is a popular flowering houseplant.

clue.text: See 17
Snack has copyright?

parts.note: having the right to copy means you can copy; can is able to
to ape is to copy

explanation.surface: A little snack bears a copyright mark?
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'has copyright' as 'is allowed to copy': CAN APE.
explanation.definitionFit: A canapé is a small savoury bite served with drinks.

clue.text: Seated uncomfortably but not inclined to move

indicators.note: sitting uncomfortably means shifting about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sitting awkwardly but reluctant to shift.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedate means calm and unhurried, not given to rushing about.

clue.text: Go it to date — not so fast!

definitions.meaning: to go it, filling the gap, means to court someone regularly
a call to slow down and keep calm

explanation.surface: Advice to a would-be suitor: hold your horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go steady' means to date one partner; 'steady!' alone is a warning to slow down.
explanation.definitionFit: The word completes the phrase for courting regularly and is also a cry urging caution.

clue.text: From two inches in five it may be split

parts.note: in is the abbreviation for inch, and two are needed

indicators.note: the inner letters go inside five

parts.note: the number five spelt out
the second inch abbreviation
taken as written

explanation.surface: A ruler-measured puzzle: a couple of inches in five, and it may be broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' is a link. Splitting this verb form, as in 'to boldly go', is a famous grammar bugbear.
explanation.definitionFit: The to-form of a verb is notoriously split by an adverb, as in 'to boldly go'.

clue.text: Pale award for acting student included without restraint

parts.note: wan means pallid

indicators.note: the award takes the learner letter inside

parts.note: a Tony is a Broadway theatre award
L is a learner, from the L-plate

explanation.surface: A pallid actor's prize, given to a student, wins it freely.
explanation.walkthrough: A Tony is the American theatre award; L is for learner, from British L-plates.
explanation.definitionFit: Wantonly means recklessly or gratuitously, without any check on behaviour.

clue.text: Fencing topped by verbal trickery

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is cut off, like a head

parts.note: swordplay is the art of fencing

explanation.surface: Fencing outdone by clever verbal tricks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fencing' suggests a garden fence; it is SWORDPLAY, and 'topped' cuts its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordplay is witty manipulation of words, as in puns.
